title: Later weather reduced held-out regional NRCS runoff error by 70% at 221 western US sites in 2006-2025
abstract: We tested whether weather after April 1 accounts for shared errors in NRCS April-July runoff forecasts. We reused a fixed panel of 221 sites in five drainage regions for 2006-2025. NOAA climate divisions supplied weather proxies at the forecast points. Regional intercepts and common precipitation and temperature slopes reduced squared regional error by 70.2% when each whole test year was left out. A bootstrap that refits the models gave 49.3-80.0% limits. Precipitation alone gave 69.7%; prior October-March weather gave no gain. A 2006-2015 fit reduced 2016-2025 error by 67.8%, but worsened the Rio Grande result. The variance of the equal-region mean error fell by 85.7%, and net cross-region covariance fell by 95.5%. The same weather model reduced squared low-tail failure error by only 28.0%; substantial shared tail variation remained. These are tests with later observed weather, not operational forecasts or causal error shares. Twenty years, selected sites, adjusted flows, archive revisions, broad weather proxies and missing issue-time weather expectations limit inference. Code, exact source hashes, aggregate evidence and a retrieval recipe are included. Raw and site-level data remain external.
